extracted.intended_audience: readers and students of philosophy, ethics, and Schopenhauerian metaphysics
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting and applying Schopenhauer's normative criteria for what counts as the 'denial of the will to live', ascetic practices, and related moral/psychological states (vs. suicide, sentimentality, temporary conversion).

rubrics_metrics.name: Denial of the will to live (definition and nature)
rubrics_metrics.description: The denial of the will to live is the extinction of willing except for the last spark that preserves the body; it is the state in which the individual 'continues to exist only as a pure, knowing being, the undimmed mirror of the world.' It is produced by knowledge which acts as a quieter of will and results in inward joy, unshakable peace, and indifference to worldly conditions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is contrasted with ordinary life (constant striving and suffering). The state is characterized by seeing life as illusion, freedom from desire, and the greatest delight in death. Examples: mystics, saints; aesthetic contemplation can give momentary glimpses, but full denial is deeper. It must be continually maintained by effort because the living body always leaves the will potentially active.

rubrics_metrics.name: Asceticism (narrow sense) as method
rubrics_metrics.description: Asceticism is defined in the narrower sense as the intentional breaking of the will by refusing what is agreeable and selecting what is disagreeable: a voluntarily chosen life of penance and self-chastisement for continual mortification of the will.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practices include voluntary renunciation of possessions, chastity, solitude, penance, and deliberately choosing disagreeable conditions. Asceticism is practised by those who have attained the denial (to preserve it) or sought as a path toward it. Examples and extreme practices from Hindu and Christian mystics are given. Asceticism must be understood as purposefully mortifying the sources of willing, not as mere suffering.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two genuine paths to denial of the will
rubrics_metrics.description: There are two primary paths: (1) the path of knowledge—penetration of the principium individuationis whereby one knows the inner conflict and vanity of willing; (2) the path of suffering—personal great suffering that breaks the will.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Schopenhauer notes that only a few attain denial by knowledge alone; most arrive via personal suffering. Distinguish whether resignation arose from intellectual insight or from suffering endured. Literary examples (e.g., Gretchen in Faust, Raymond Lully) illustrate the suffering path. The difference matters for evaluating authenticity and permanence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aesthetic contemplation as a temporary quieter of the will
rubrics_metrics.description: Aesthetic pleasure in the beautiful temporarily lifts one above all willing: 'in entering the state of pure contemplation we are lifted for the moment above all willing... we become... freed from ourselves.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such moments are fleeting and not equivalent to the permanent denial of the will; they show the possibility and desirability of the quieter state but do not substitute for ascetic renunciation or the deeper knowledge required for lasting denial.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suicide is an assertion of will, not denial
rubrics_metrics.description: Suicide differs fundamentally from the denial of the will to live: it is a phenomenon of strong assertion of will because the suicide still wills life (or the cessation of particular conditions) and destroys only the individual manifestation, not the will itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Suicide is morally and metaphysically vain and foolish because it removes only the single phenomenal existence while leaving the will unaffected. It is contrasted with the ascetic who shuns joys rather than sorrows. Schopenhauer therefore rejects suicide as a path to salvation; the genuine way is through knowledge or allowing suffering to produce resignation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Voluntary starvation as exceptional case
rubrics_metrics.description: There exists a form of death by voluntary starvation undertaken from extreme ascetic resignation; in such cases the person may have 'altogether ceased to will' and thus may die because no will remains to take nourishment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These cases are rare and often entangled with religious fanaticism or insanity; historical examples are cited. If genuine, such death differs from ordinary suicide because it results from an absence of will rather than its assertion; still, accounts are ambiguous and debated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suffering as potentially sanctifying only if universalized
rubrics_metrics.description: All suffering has potentially a sanctifying power, but it truly inspires reverence only when the sufferer raises his view from the particular circumstances to the universal—regarding his suffering as example of the whole rather than clinging to its specific cause.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If suffering is contemplated as an instance of the universal vanity and conflict of will, it can lead to resignation; if it remains tied to a particular grievance or hope, it will not. Literary/philosophical examples (Torquato Tasso, Petrarch) illustrate when suffering produces genuine resigned character versus when it produces mere complaint or sentimentality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Signs of genuine resignation/holiness
rubrics_metrics.description: True resignation is accompanied by inward joy, deep unshaken peace, serenity, willingness to renounce previous desires, indifference to worldly forms, and a 'great delight in death.' The resigned person views life as a fleeting illusion and experiences freedom from desire.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These signs distinguish authentic denial from mere external markers or ostentation. The resigned person often intentionally embraces disagreeable circumstances to preserve the state; their apparent poverty or privation coexists with inner bliss. Examples include mystics and saints whose inward life aligns with these features.

rubrics_metrics.name: Danger of sentimentality versus true resignation
rubrics_metrics.description: Sentimentality is the unhealthy condition of always mourning and lamenting without rising courageously to resignation; it results in losing both earth and heaven and produces only 'watery sentimentality.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluators should distinguish between noble, quiet sadness arising from universal knowledge and base, constant fretfulness or indulgent melancholy. In artistic representation, sentimentality is an anti-pattern: mourning without the transformation into resignation is inauthentic and spiritually empty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Resignation requires continual battle; it is not permanently secure
rubrics_metrics.description: Even after the denial of the will has once appeared, it wavers and must be ever anew attained by a constant battle, because the living body keeps the will potentially active and desire can reassert itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This criterion implies that durability and ongoing practice (ascetic discipline, penance, selective avoidance of pleasures) are part of evaluating a true resigned life. Temporary conversions that revert when suffering ends are common; stability over time is a mark of depth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Durability vs. temporary conversions
rubrics_metrics.description: Conversions to resignation produced by misfortune or prison/illness are sometimes temporary; the true test is whether the change persists beyond the occasion of suffering.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples (Benvenuto Cellini, others) show reversion to former life once suffering ceases. Assess authenticity by examining whether the person, after recovery of comfort or health, maintains the reoriented willlessness or falls back to previous volitions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral guidance: promote nature's aims to allow salvation
rubrics_metrics.description: Schopenhauer argues that one must promote the aims of Nature (life's continuation and manifestation) because only by allowing the will to manifest unrestrictedly in individuals can it, through knowledge gained in such manifestation, transcend itself and attain salvation; killing germ or newborn to prevent suffering is impossible path to salvation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This functions as a practical ethical criterion: policies or actions that prematurely destroy life (to avert suffering) are misguided; instead, facilitate life so that the will may be educated toward knowledge and denial. This also informs the moral condemnation of filicide or preventing birth out of pity for suffering.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explanation of murder-suicide motive as metaphysical delusion
rubrics_metrics.description: When suicide extends to killing one's children before oneself, the act is explained as the father's mistaken attempt to end the will as a whole by destroying related manifestations in which he recognizes himself; it reflects delusion rather than valid negation of will.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This entry functions as an explanatory criterion for evaluating such acts: they are not proper denial but a confused, metaphysically mistaken attempt to annihilate manifestation rather than attain knowledge. It reinforces Schopenhauer's rejection of violent means to accomplish metaphysical ends.
